title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
gist: Casey Crownhart previews COP31 in Antalya, Turkey (Nov 8–20, 2026), cohosted by Turkey and Australia. The talks are overshadowed by the Iran war's energy shock, US absence, a 1.5 °C goal set to be breached, a large climate-finance shortfall and weakening fossil-fuel language. The presidency is adding a toothless AI-sustainability pledge and a target for electricity to reach 35% of energy use by 2035.

insights.claim: COP31, the 2026 UN climate talks, opened November 8 in Antalya, Turkey, cohosted by Turkey and Australia and scheduled to end November 20, with fossil fuels and climate finance expected to be the most contested topics.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Watch late-November final text for fossil-fuel and finance language as a sentiment signal for energy-transition policy.
insights.quote: expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular
insights.locator: It's that time of year again

insights.claim: The ongoing war in Iran has disrupted the Middle East and spiked global energy prices, making the 2026 COP31 climate talks especially charged.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Energy-security pressures from the Iran war may push negotiators toward supply concerns over decarbonization ambition.
insights.locator: In recent years, the tension always feels high

insights.claim: The US has no formal delegation at COP31 for the second year running, after President Trump withdrew from the Paris Agreement and began withdrawing from the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change treaty that enables formal participation.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: US absence weakens finance commitments and leaves multilateral climate policy to other blocs; US climate policy risk stays tilted away from federal support.
insights.locator: This year's COP will be the second without a formal delegation

insights.claim: A September 2026 UN Environment Program report acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C goal, likely within the next few years.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Overshoot of 1.5 °C shifts emphasis toward adaptation spending and physical-risk exposure in asset pricing.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, things aren't looking good for the Paris Agreement

insights.claim: COP29 set a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 for emissions reduction and climate adaptation, while OECD data show rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, less than half the target.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A gap of over $160 billion a year to the 2035 target shows how far climate-finance flows still fall short of pledges.
insights.locator: Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion

insights.claim: The COP30 agreement in 2025 set a goal of tripling adaptation finance by 2035, even though adaptation funding has been roughly flat for several years.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Adaptation-focused infrastructure and resilience providers have a stated policy tailwind, but past funding trends suggest delivery risk.
insights.quote: Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.
insights.locator: And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling

insights.claim: A 2026 Himalayan glacier-collapse flood killed about 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing and caused nearly $5 billion in damage, yet the UN loss and damages fund committed only $20 million to Nepal, less than 1% of the estimated cost.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Loss-and-damage mechanisms are badly underfunded compared with real climate disasters, which strengthens the case for insurance and resilience demand.
insights.locator: The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are

insights.claim: UN climate agreement text on fossil fuels has regressed: the COP28 deal explicitly called for transitioning away from fossil fuels, but the COP30 final agreement did not mention the phrase 'fossil fuels' at all.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Weakening multilateral language on fossil fuels lowers near-term policy risk for oil, gas and coal producers.
insights.quote: the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once
insights.locator: Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations

insights.claim: Both COP31 cohosts depend on fossil fuels: Australia is a major coal and natural gas exporter, and Turkey's power grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal, which raises doubts about how ambitious the COP31 fossil-fuel text will be.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Host-country fossil exposure suggests a low chance of strong phase-out language from COP31.
insights.locator: This will be an interesting conversation

themes.theme: Presidency side pledges: AI and electrification

insights.claim: COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, is promoting a voluntary pledge to make AI more sustainable that explicitly creates no new obligations for countries, so it is unenforceable.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Do not expect binding climate constraints on AI data-center buildout from COP31; the AI-energy demand story is effectively unconstrained by this pledge.
insights.quote: this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go
insights.locator: One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable

insights.claim: The COP31 leadership is pushing a pledge for electricity to make up 35% of total global energy consumption by 2035, up from about 23% today, with fossil fuels such as gasoline in vehicles and natural gas for heating making up most of the rest.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A 23% to 35% electrification target points to sustained demand for grid equipment, EVs, heat pumps and clean generation.
insights.locator: The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity

insights.claim: The author expects no breakthrough from COP31 despite organizers calling it an 'implementation COP,' signaling low expectations for tangible progress on climate action.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Markets should not price meaningful policy upside from COP31; treat any strong outcome as an upside surprise.
insights.locator: With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,”
